questions.q: Turn the current folder into a new Git repository.
questions.explain: `git init` creates the hidden .git directory that stores the whole history.

questions.q: Download a full copy of https://github.com/netrealm/configs.git
questions.output:
Cloning into 'configs'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 412, done.
Receiving objects: 100% (412/412), 88.3 KiB | 2.1 MiB/s, done.
questions.explain: `git clone` copies the repository including its full history and sets up `origin` as the remote.

questions.q: See which files are modified, staged or untracked.
questions.output:
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  modified:   routers/r1.cfg
Untracked files:
  switches/sw9.cfg
questions.explain: `git status` is the command you'll run most. `git status -s` gives a compact view.

questions.q: Stage ALL changes in the repo (new, modified and deleted files) for the next commit.
questions.explain: `git add .` stages everything under the current directory; `git add -A` stages everything in the repo. Stage individual files with `git add path/file`.

questions.q: Commit the staged changes with the message: fix dns
questions.output:
[main 7c3e91a] fix dns
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
questions.explain: Commits snapshot the staged changes. Good messages are short, imperative and explain WHY: 'Fix DNS forwarder on R1 after ISP change'.

questions.q: Create a new branch named feature/vlan and switch to it in one command.
questions.explain: `git switch -c` is the modern form; `git checkout -b` is the classic one. Branches are cheap, so use one per change.

questions.q: Push the new local branch feature/vlan to origin for the first time AND set it as upstream.
questions.output:
To github.com:netrealm/configs.git
 * [new branch]      feature/vlan -> feature/vlan
branch 'feature/vlan' set up to track 'origin/feature/vlan'.
questions.explain: `-u` (`--set-upstream`) links the local branch to the remote one, so later a plain `git push` or `git pull` just works.

questions.q: Show the commit history, one commit per line.
questions.output:
7c3e91a (HEAD -> main) fix dns
2b8d1f0 Add VLAN 30 to access switches
91aa4c2 Initial import of router configs
questions.explain: `git log --oneline` gives a compact view. Add `--graph --all` to visualize branches.

questions.q: Fetch the latest changes from the remote AND merge them into your current branch.
patterns: git pull( origin main| origin master| --rebase| --ff-only)?
questions.explain: `git pull` = `git fetch` + `git merge` (or rebase with `--rebase`). `git fetch` alone downloads without touching your working branch.

questions.q: Merge the branch feature/vlan into the current branch (main).
questions.explain: `git merge` brings another branch's commits into the current one. Fast-forward if possible, otherwise it creates a merge commit.

questions.q: Show the line-by-line changes you've made but NOT yet staged.
questions.output:
--- a/routers/r1.cfg
+++ b/routers/r1.cfg
@@ -12,7 +12,7 @@
- ip name-server 8.8.8.8
+ ip name-server 10.0.0.53
questions.explain: `git diff` = working tree vs staging area. `git diff --staged` = staging area vs last commit.

questions.q: Temporarily shelve your uncommitted changes so you can switch branches with a clean tree.
questions.output: Saved working directory and index state WIP on feature/vlan: 5f2c7aa Add VLAN 30
questions.explain: `git stash` saves your work on a stack; `git stash pop` restores it. Add `-u` to include untracked files.

questions.q: Commit a1b2c3d broke production and is already pushed to the shared main branch. Undo it SAFELY by creating a new commit that reverses it.
questions.hint: Don't rewrite shared history: git re...
questions.output:
[main 9d0e3f1] Revert "Change OSPF cost on core links"
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
questions.explain: `git revert` adds a new commit that undoes the old one, so history stays intact for everyone. `git reset` rewrites history: avoid it on shared branches.

questions.q: Switch to the existing branch named main.
questions.output:
Switched to branch 'main'
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
questions.explain: `git switch main` (modern) or `git checkout main` (classic).

questions.q: What is Continuous Integration (CI)?
choices: Merging small changes often, with every change automatically built and tested
Deploying straight to production with no tests
Writing all code on one long-lived branch for months
Manually testing before each yearly release
questions.explain: CI catches integration problems early: every push triggers an automated build plus tests, so main is always in a known-good state.

questions.q: Continuous DELIVERY vs continuous DEPLOYMENT: what's the difference?
choices: Delivery keeps every change releasable but needs a manual approval to go live; deployment ships automatically
Deployment needs manual approval; delivery is automatic
Delivery is for networks, deployment is for servers
questions.explain: Both automate the pipeline up to production. Continuous deployment removes the final human gate: if all tests pass, it ships.

questions.q: What is a pull request (merge request) for?
choices: Proposing changes from a branch so they can be reviewed and tested before merging
questions.explain: PRs enable code review, discussion and automated CI checks, and branch protection can require approvals before merge.

questions.q: What's the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
choices: fetch downloads remote changes without merging; pull fetches AND merges
pull downloads without merging; fetch merges
questions.explain: `git fetch` updates remote-tracking branches (origin/main) safely. `git pull` then integrates them into your current branch.

questions.q: What does `git rebase main` do while on a feature branch?
choices: Replays your feature commits on top of the latest main, giving a linear history
Merges main with a merge commit
questions.explain: Rebase rewrites your commits so they start from main's tip. That's clean, but it changes commit IDs, so don't rebase commits others have already pulled.

questions.q: When should you NOT rebase?
choices: On commits already pushed to a shared branch others are using
On your local, unpushed feature branch
questions.explain: The golden rule: don't rewrite public history. Rebasing shared commits forces everyone else into painful recoveries.

questions.q: What is the .gitignore file for?
choices: Listing files and patterns Git should NOT track (secrets, build output...)
questions.explain: e.g. `*.log`, `.env`, `node_modules/`. Note: it won't untrack files already committed, so remove them with `git rm --cached`.

questions.q: When does a merge conflict happen?
choices: Both branches changed the same lines of a file differently
A file was added on one branch
questions.explain: Git can't decide which version wins, so it marks the file with <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> and you resolve it by hand.

questions.q: Where do GitHub Actions workflow files live in a repository?
questions.explain: Any .yml/.yaml file in .github/workflows/ is a workflow. (This very game deploys to GitHub Pages using one!)

questions.q: In a GitHub Actions workflow, what does `on: push` define?
choices: The event that triggers the workflow
questions.explain: `on:` lists triggers: push, pull_request, schedule (cron), workflow_dispatch (manual button), and more.

questions.q: What does `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` specify?
choices: The type of runner machine the job executes on
questions.explain: Each job runs on a fresh runner: GitHub-hosted (ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest) or self-hosted.

questions.q: A job has `needs: [test]`. What does that do?
choices: The job waits until the 'test' job succeeds
It installs a package called test
It runs in parallel with test
questions.explain: `needs` creates dependencies between jobs (e.g. build → test → deploy). Without it, jobs run in parallel.

questions.q: What is a blue/green deployment?
choices: Two identical environments; deploy to the idle one, then switch all traffic over (and back if needed)
Updating servers one at a time
Sending 5% of users to the new version first
questions.explain: Blue/green gives near-instant cutover and rollback, at the cost of double the infrastructure.

questions.q: What is a canary release?
choices: Ship the new version to a small slice of users first, watch metrics, then expand
questions.explain: Like the canary in a coal mine: if the small group sees errors, you stop before everyone is affected.

questions.q: A rolling deployment:
choices: Replaces instances gradually, a few at a time, while the rest keep serving
questions.explain: Kubernetes Deployments roll by default (maxSurge/maxUnavailable). Old and new versions run side by side briefly.

questions.q: What is a build artifact?
choices: The output of a build stage (binary, package, container image) stored for later stages
questions.explain: Build once, promote the SAME artifact through test, staging and production. Rebuilding for each environment risks differences.

questions.q: How should a pipeline use an API key?
choices: Store it in the CI secret store and reference it, e.g. ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}
Hardcode it in the workflow YAML
Print it in the logs for debugging
questions.explain: Secrets stores encrypt values and mask them in logs. If a key ever lands in Git history, rotate it: deleting the file isn't enough.

questions.q: What must YAML use for indentation?
questions.explain: YAML structure IS indentation, and tabs are illegal. Most pipeline failures at 2 AM are a single misplaced space.

questions.q: Trunk-based development means:
choices: Everyone integrates small changes into main frequently, using short-lived branches
Each feature lives on a branch for months
questions.explain: Short-lived branches plus frequent merges mean fewer conflicts (the Merge Conflict Hydra starves!). Feature flags hide unfinished work.

questions.q: In semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH), a backwards-compatible BUG FIX bumps:
questions.explain: PATCH = bug fixes, MINOR = new backwards-compatible features, MAJOR = breaking changes.

questions.q: Why is `git reset --hard` dangerous?
choices: It permanently discards uncommitted changes in your working tree
It can't be run on main
questions.explain: Uncommitted work is gone for good (committed work can often be recovered with `git reflog`). Consider `git stash` first.

questions.q: In Git, what is HEAD?
choices: A pointer to the commit/branch you currently have checked out
questions.explain: HEAD normally points at a branch, which points at a commit. 'Detached HEAD' means it points straight at a commit: create a branch before committing there!

questions.q: What does 'shift left' mean in DevOps?
choices: Move testing and security checks earlier in the development pipeline
Move servers to the left rack
questions.explain: Bugs and vulnerabilities are cheaper to fix the earlier you find them: linting, unit tests and SAST in CI, not after release.

questions.q: What is a unit test?
choices: A fast test of one small piece of code in isolation
A test of the whole system in production
questions.explain: The testing pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few slow end-to-end tests.

questions.q: What does a linter do?
choices: Statically checks code or config for errors and style issues without running it
questions.explain: Examples: yamllint, ansible-lint, flake8, shellcheck. Run them in CI to catch mistakes before review.

questions.q: Order the basic Git workflow for shipping a change.
questions.explain: Working tree → staging area (add) → local repo (commit) → remote (push) → review & merge (PR).

questions.q: Order the typical stages of a CI/CD pipeline.
questions.explain: Each stage gates the next. A failing test stops the pipeline before anything reaches production.

questions.q: Order the feature-branch workflow.
questions.explain: Branch → commit → PR → review + green CI → merge → clean up. Branch protection rules can enforce the review and CI steps.

questions.q: What is the exact filename that tells Git which files to ignore?
questions.explain: `.gitignore`, with the leading dot. It can live in the repo root or any subdirectory.

questions.q: Which directory path holds GitHub Actions workflow files? (relative to the repo root)
questions.explain: .github/workflows/: every YAML file there defines a workflow.

questions.q: Your tool is at version 2.4.1. You add a NEW backwards-compatible feature. What's the new version?
questions.explain: MINOR bump → 2.5.0. Bumping MINOR resets PATCH to 0.

questions.q: Your tool is at version 2.4.1. You make a BREAKING API change. What's the new version?
questions.explain: MAJOR bump → 3.0.0. Bumping MAJOR resets MINOR and PATCH to 0.

questions.q: In GitHub Actions, what does `uses: actions/checkout@v4` do in a step?
choices: Runs a reusable action that checks out your repository onto the runner
Checks out a pull request for review
questions.explain: `uses:` runs a published action at a pinned version. Without checkout, the runner has an empty workspace. `run:` executes shell commands instead.

questions.q: Which of these is a Git conflict marker?
questions.explain: Conflicts look like `<<<<<<< HEAD` (yours), `=======`, then `>>>>>>> branch` (theirs). Edit to the final version, delete the markers, `git add`, then commit.
